title: Events
summary: Let one object announce that something happened, without knowing who is listening.

steps.title: Delegates, one more time
body: A **delegate** is a type that holds methods. You already know the built-in ones, `Action` and `Func`. You can also declare your own, which gives the shape a name:
delegate void PriceChanged(string symbol, decimal price);
A delegate variable can hold **more than one** method. `+=` adds a method to the list, `-=` removes one. Calling the delegate calls every method in it, in the order they were added.
PriceChanged onChange = (symbol, price) => Console.WriteLine($"{symbol} is now {price}");
That is the whole mechanism behind events: a list of methods to call when something happens.

code: Action<string> notify = name => Console.WriteLine("Email to " + name);
steps.explain: One call runs every method in the delegate, in the order they were added with `+=`.

steps.title: The event keyword
body: A doorbell could expose its listeners as a public delegate:
public Action? Rang;          // a public delegate field
That works, but it trusts every outsider far too much. Any code anywhere can do `bell.Rang = null;` and wipe out everyone else's subscriptions, or call `bell.Rang()` and fake a ring.
Add one word, `event`, and the compiler locks it down:
From **outside** the class, an event allows exactly two things: `+=` (subscribe) and `-=` (unsubscribe). Only the class that owns the event can raise it or clear it.

steps.prompt: `Doorbell` declares `public event Action? Rang;`. Each line below is written **outside** the `Doorbell` class. Does it compile?
steps.explain: Outsiders may only subscribe and unsubscribe. Assigning and invoking are reserved for the class that declares the event.

steps.title: EventHandler<T> and raising safely
body: Almost every .NET event uses the same delegate shape, so you rarely declare your own:
- `EventHandler<T>` means *a method taking `(object? sender, T e)`*. `sender` is the object that raised the event, `e` is the data.
- With nothing to report, use plain `EventHandler` and pass `EventArgs.Empty`.
- An event with **no subscribers is `null`**. Calling it directly would throw `NullReferenceException`. `?.Invoke(...)` calls it only when someone is listening.

steps.prompt: Complete the class so that it compiles and `Dispatch` is safe to call even when nobody has subscribed.
steps.explain: `event` restricts outsiders to `+=` and `-=`. `?.Invoke` skips the call when the event is null. `this` is the sender.

`Report` must not crash when nobody is subscribed.

Raise it with `Overheated?.Invoke(sender, data)`. The `?.` covers the no-subscribers case.

steps.title: Unsubscribing, and the leak you get if you forget
body: A subscription is a reference **from the publisher to the subscriber**. As long as the publisher is alive, it keeps every subscriber alive too, and keeps calling them.

So a short-lived object that subscribes to a long-lived one must unsubscribe when it is done. Otherwise it is never garbage collected, and it keeps reacting to events it no longer cares about. This is the most common memory leak in .NET.
void OnClick(object? sender, EventArgs e) => Console.WriteLine("clicked");
button.Clicked -= OnClick;    // removes it: same method, same target
`-=` removes a handler that is *equal* to the one you pass. A named method is equal to itself. Two lambdas are never equal, even with identical text:
> **Tip:** If you will ever need to unsubscribe, subscribe with a named method, or keep the lambda in a variable.

code: void OnClick(object? sender, EventArgs e) => Console.WriteLine("clicked");
steps.explain: Subscribing twice means being called twice. One `-=` removes one subscription, so one remains.

steps.title: The member who never leaves
prompt: A `Member` joins a `ChatRoom` and collects every message in `Inbox`. After `Leave`, the member should hear nothing more.
Right now Ben keeps receiving messages after he leaves, and the room keeps him alive forever. Find out why `Leave` removes nothing, and fix `Member`.
starter: public void Post(string text) => MessagePosted?.Invoke(this, text);
solution: public void Post(string text) => MessagePosted?.Invoke(this, text);
private void OnMessage(object? sender, string text) => Inbox.Add(text);
template: Dojo.Eq("Ana, who stayed, hears both messages", "hello | anyone there?", string.Join(" | ", ana.Inbox));
Dojo.Eq("Ben hears nothing after he leaves", "hello", string.Join(" | ", ben.Inbox));
Dojo.Eq("The room has one subscriber left", 1, room.SubscriberCount);
hints: `-=` only removes a handler equal to the one that was added. Is the lambda in `Leave` the same object as the lambda in `Join`?
Move the handler into a named method: `private void OnMessage(object? sender, string text) => Inbox.Add(text);`
Then `Join` does `room.MessagePosted += OnMessage;` and `Leave` does `room.MessagePosted -= OnMessage;`.

steps.title: Sidekick celebrates
prompt: **Sidekick piece: celebrations.** When you run `sk done 3`, Sidekick cheers. The task code does not know about cheering: it only raises an event, and whoever cares subscribes. Your `TaskItem` is given.
1. `TaskEvents` with `public event Action<TaskItem>? Completed;` and `public void RaiseCompleted(TaskItem task)`, which raises it (safe when nobody listens).
2. `Celebrations : IDisposable`, constructor `Celebrations(TaskEvents events, Action<string> say)`. It subscribes to `Completed` and counts completions. For each one it calls `say` with:
`Dispose()` unsubscribes, so a disposed `Celebrations` hears nothing (and the events object no longer keeps it alive).
template: Dojo.Try("raising with nobody listening is safe", () => dojoEvents.RaiseCompleted(new TaskItem(99, "Nobody listens")));
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) dojoEvents.RaiseCompleted(new TaskItem(i + 1, dojoTitles[i]));
Dojo.Eq("the first completion", "First one down: Fix login", dojoSaid.ElementAtOrDefault(0));
Dojo.Eq("an ordinary one says the count", "Done: Write tests (2 so far)", dojoSaid.ElementAtOrDefault(1));
Dojo.Eq("the third", "Three done. You're on a roll!", dojoSaid.ElementAtOrDefault(2));
Dojo.Eq("the fourth", "Done: Deploy (4 so far)", dojoSaid.ElementAtOrDefault(3));
Dojo.Eq("the fifth", "Five! Take a real break.", dojoSaid.ElementAtOrDefault(4));
Dojo.Eq("after Dispose it hears nothing", 10, dojoSaid.Count);
Dojo.Eq("two listeners both hear, and both leave", "1 1", $"{dojoA.Count} {dojoB.Count}");
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
hints: `public void RaiseCompleted(TaskItem task) => Completed?.Invoke(task);` The `?.` makes it safe with no subscribers.
Keep `events` and `say` in fields and subscribe a *method* (`events.Completed += OnCompleted;`), so `Dispose` can remove exactly that method.
In `OnCompleted`: `count++;` then `say(count switch { 1 => $"First one down: {task.Title}", 3 => ..., _ => $"Done: {task.Title} ({count} so far)" });`.
steps.explain: A lambda subscribed with `+=` can never be removed, because you have no second reference to it. A method group can: `-= OnCompleted` finds the same method on the same object. That is the leak from the last exercise, fixed on purpose.
